full_content: President Donald Trumpsays he’s willing to further extend the deadline for TikTok to sell itself or be banned in America. Trump had already given TikTok, which is owned by China-based ByteDance, a 75-day extension in April. The president said he has “a little warm spot” in his heart for the app, which became a key platform for him during last year’s presidential run. Congress passed a bill forcing ByteDance to sell off TikTok’s U.S. operations to an American company last year, and President Joe Biden signed it into law. But Trump’s reelection has offered a reprieve to TikTok even as it has seemedto get caught upin the mounting trade war between the U.S. and China.

full_content: Warren Buffett plansto retire from Berkshire Hathaway at the end of the year and hopes his longtime heir apparent will take his place running the conglomerate, Buffett said in an unexpected announcement at Berkshire’s annual shareholder meeting on Saturday. Buffett will recommend to Berkshire’s board that the company’s vice chairman, Greg Abel, replaces him. Buffett had anointed Abel as his preferred successor back in 2021, and he was already running all of Berkshire’s non-insurance business. Nonetheless, Buffett’s announcement was a surprise, since even at age 94, Buffett had given no indication that he had any plans to retire. In building up Berkshire over decades, Buffett largely eschewed investing in tech companies, which he saw as too complicated and too susceptible to fast-paced change. Still, he made an exception for Apple, and on Saturday, Apple CEO Tim Cook wasted no time in singing Buffett’s praises. “There’s never been anyone like Warren,” Cookwroteon X.

title: Apple Plans iPhone Release Schedule Shakeup, New Styles
feed_content:
After years of incremental changes to the iPhone, Apple is mixing things up much more dramatically. Later this year it’s expected to introduce an ultrathin new device, followed by a foldable phone expected in 2026. Also next year, Apple plans to change its release strategy, launching pricier, more premium versions in the fall as usual, but pushing the release of the more affordable standard model to the following spring.

Apple’s hope is to rejuvenate long-stagnant sales of the iPhone, its flagship product, which accounts for more than half its revenue. But there are risks involved in the upcoming changes. The level of consumer demand for the new thin iPhone is so uncertain that Apple’s manufacturing partners in Asia are dedicating only about 10% of their production capacity to the new model, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter.
full_content: After years ofincremental changes to the iPhone, Apple is mixing things up much more dramatically. Later this year it’s expected to introduce an ultrathin new device, followed by a foldable phone expected in 2026. Also next year, Apple plans to change its release strategy, launching pricier, more premium versions in the fall as usual, but pushing the release of the more affordable standard model to the following spring. Apple’s hope is to rejuvenate long-stagnant sales of the iPhone, its flagship product, which accounts for more than half its revenue. But there are risks involved in the upcoming changes. The level of consumer demand for the new thin iPhone is so uncertain that Apple’s manufacturing partners in Asia are dedicating only about 10% of their production capacity to the new model, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. They’re reserving most of their production for the iPhone 17 Pro Max and Pro, which will account for around 40% and 25% of total production, respectively, the people said. The rest will be reserved for the standard iPhone 17 model. While Apple hasn’t confirmed plans for the new thin model, it is expected to be around 5.5 millimeters in thickness, which would be the thinnest phone the company has ever released and one of the thinnest smartphones currently on the market. Apple’s hope is likely that the new model will prompt people to upgrade faster, overcoming the problem that users are holding onto their smartphones for much longer nowadays than they used to, largely because most annual upgrades bring only minor changes. However, the smaller size of the new thin model will require compromises to its capabilities. The device will contain only a single speaker instead of the two speakers that Apple’s other phones usually have, one rear camera lens instead of the three in Apple’s flagship phones, and reduced battery life. Internal testing shows that battery life for the thin model will fall short of that of previous iPhones. The percentage of users who can go a single day without recharging the thin phone will be between 60% and 70%. For other models, that metric is between 80% and 90%, one of the people said. To solve this, Apple is developing an optional accessory—a phone case meant for the thin model that also contains a battery pack, according to three people familiar with the matter. Apple could face challenges selling the thin iPhone in China, as the model doesn’t have space for physical SIM cards. Chinese regulations have yet to approve the sale of smartphones that rely on electronic SIMs, The Information previouslyreported. One of the people said that until preorders start in September, it’s impossible to predict whether the manufacturing lines the manufacturers are setting up will be enough or even over capacity for the thin iPhone, given that it’s an entirely new product with no historical demand to reference. For all these reasons, manufacturers reserving production capacity for the phone are looking at how quickly they can convert their manufacturing lines to other models if the thin model doesn’t sell well, two people said. An Apple spokesperson declined to comment. New Release Window Release of the thin iPhone will mark the start of a bigger shift in Apple’s iPhone planning. Next year, Apple plans to release its first foldable iPhone, The Information previouslyreported. The book-style foldable device will have an inner display measuring just under 8 inches diagonally when unfolded and an outer display of just under 5.7 inches diagonally when shut, according to a person involved in its manufacturing. Also next year, Apple plans to stagger the release of its iPhone by only releasing the premium, more expensive Pro models in the fall and delaying the standard iPhone model—in this case the iPhone 18—until the following spring, according to three people involved in the iPhone supply chain. The iPhone 18 series will include updated versions of Apple’s thin iPhone, Pro and Pro Max, along with the new foldable device. In spring 2027, Apple plans to release the standard iPhone 18 and a successor to the more budget-friendly iPhone 16e, the people said. Both those models, which are based on older and less complicated designs, will undergo manufacturing trials first in India as part of Apple’s efforts to reduce its manufacturing risk in China, two of the people said. The change to the iPhone’s release window could make it easier for Apple to ramp up production of an increasing number of different phones. By staggering the launch, Apple can reduce the need to deploy large numbers of manufacturing workers and equipment simultaneously. Those who have worked in Apple’s supply chain say production of new iPhones begins in the summer to build up inventory ahead of a fall release, and orders peak just before winter, due to the holiday shopping season. Production begins to taper off the following January, making it difficult for Apple’s manufacturing partners to keep the same amount of workers and equipment operating year-round. Apple releases its cheapest smartphone in the spring, though it updates that model only once every few years. In February, for instance, it released the iPhone 16e, the successor to the iPhone SE. Global demand for iPhones has slowed over the past two years. Apple’s iPhone sales in fiscal 2023 were down more than 2% year over year, and sales in fiscal 2024 and the first half of fiscal 2025 were essentially flat year over year. Delaying the launch of the next-generation base iPhone by five or six months after releasing the more premium iPhones could lift sales. “Front-loading the more premium models early and releasing the lower-end models later might get early adopters to buy the more expensive models first,” said Horace Dediu, founder at market analysis firm Asymco. Other Notable Changes One of the more significant changes to the iPhone lineup could arrive in 2026, when Apple likely plans to move its Face ID, proximity and light sensors beneath the display—bringing it closer to offering a fully uninterrupted screen, free of the unsightly pill-shaped cutout at the top. Apple wouldn’t be the first smartphone maker to integrate sensors and cameras under the display, though the results haven’t been great for many of the Chinese smartphone makers at the forefront of this trend. The design of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will include only a small hole cutout in the top-left corner to accommodate the front-facing camera, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. This design is a precursor to at least one 2027 iPhone model that will place the front-facing camera underneath the screen to enable a truly edge-to-edge display, two of the people said. Such a move would coincide with the 20-year anniversary of the first iPhone. Some details of Apple’s foldable phone were first mentioned by supply chain analyst Ming-Chi Kuo in March, while the timetable for under-the-display cameras and sensors was firstmentionedby analysts at Display Supply Chain Consultants in 2023. Qianer Liu contributed to this article. Wayne Ma is a reporter covering U.S. tech in Asia, from Apple's supply chain to Facebook's and Google's operations in the region. He previously worked for The Wall Street Journal. He is based in Hong Kong and can be found on Twitter at@waynema.

title: What’s Bad About a Nice Robot?
feed_content:
Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter:

• The Arena: Why sports leagues learned to love creators and stop fighting them

• The Top 5: The startups hoping for a “MAHA” boom

• Power and Influence: Tech’s Trumpists have no regrets 

• Plus, our Recommendations: A sinister snafu; when India changed the world; Amy Sherman-Palladino strikes back

Why can’t we have nice things? 

Because they give us the willies, apparently. OpenAI has undone part of the latest update to its GPT‑4o model after people complained about the personality built into it, which seemed overly fawning. I’m still chuckling after my conversation with Kristian Hammond, a Northwestern University computer science professor, about why we get unsettled by such behavior. He brought up a particular fictional character.

“Eddie Haskell from ‘Leave It to Beaver,’ the kid who lived across the street,” said Hammond. “He would come over and be like, ‘Oh, you’re looking so lovely today, Mrs. Cleaver.’ And it was clear he was just, like, an irritating asshole because he was being nice in an extreme way.”

To a large degree, I think our discomfort with the model’s behavior says as much about us humans as it does about the bots we’re building. Very honestly, I think it reflects our general discomfort with positive feedback, which we don’t dispense to each other in great amounts. (Probably that reality warrants a little more self-reflection.) And because the model’s behavior seemed quite unhumanlike, that reminded us it isn’t close to being human. It gives us the icks, making us less eager to use it—it’s some version of the uncanny valley effect that’s more visually apparent when Dall-E generates some six-nosed monstrosity. 

I’m pretty sure I noticed the model’s personality change several days before OpenAI made this change. (To me, the persona read as “millennial bro,” which I suppose is what Eddie Haskell would be in modern terms.) I didn’t like it, but I also had no desire to curb my growing ChatGPT use, so I simply asked the bot to drop the act. It complied. That OpenAI felt compelled to take apart the model en masse tells me it has considerable work to do in educating users on how they can use its products and, more generally, in making its products more usable.

OpenAI is far from the only AI company with bad design. I actually can’t think of any product in the industry that is well designed. Most of it is about as sophisticated as word processing in the 1980s, and even that might be an optimistic conclusion.

As far as improving the bots’ personalities, the task will take some considerable time to get there, Hammond cautioned me. That’s simply because there isn’t a vast amount of existing written work to use in model training that would reflect what we ideally want from a bot: polite, courteous, friendly—humanish but nothing maximalistic. “We don’t have the right data to teach it to be ‘normal.’ How do you identify what ‘normal’ is? The extremes are easier. Getting to the middle of the road is tough,” Hammond said. 

Josh Kushner, a Warren Buffett in the Making?

I don’t like to be the type of person who goes around saying, ‘I told you so!’ But as my former colleague Kate Clark and I did point out a few years ago, the most interesting fella in venture capital continues to be Thrive Capital’s Josh Kushner. 

He’s always doing it all. Helping Sam Altman finish mountainous amounts of fundraising. Buying Life magazine. And now launching a new part of Thrive called Thrive Holdings, which, as the name suggests, intends to buy and hold companies for “the long term,” as Kushner wrote on X. 

I’m fascinated to know exactly what Kushner means by “long term.” (He wouldn’t comment for this column.) It could mean anything, and I detect a real strategy in leaving it totally undefined. Doing so gives Kushner real flexibility with finding investors: Unlike those in VC, they presumably won’t expect Thrive Holdings to show bountiful returns anytime soon. 

I’m also fascinated to know exactly what type of companies he plans to acquire. Kushner has left that part of his plan open-ended, too. If they’re tech companies, he’ll have his work cut out for him. There’s a reason why Warren Buffett, the grand poobah of buying and holding, famously doesn’t invest much in tech—largely because many tech companies don’t have much of what Buffett famously calls a “moat,” a well-fortified competitive advantage, as more traditional businesses do. The tech industry courses with immense, fast-paced change. In 2005, everyone seemed to have a BlackBerry. By 2015, almost no one did. Yet then as now, plenty of moms will receive See’s Candies for Mother’s Day, which helps explain why Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway has owned that company since 1972. 

If Thrive Holdings does make money by buying up tech businesses and adopts Buffett’s preferred investing time horizon—forever—or one close to it, Kushner would end up showing how wrongheaded Buffett has been for the past several decades. No easy feat!—Abram Brown

This week we welcome a brand-new addition to The Information’s Tech Sports Team Owners Database, as Sukhinder Singh Cassidy has joined the ownership of the WNBA’s Toronto Tempo. A longtime Bay Area resident and native Canadian, Singh Cassidy is currently CEO of Xero, an accounting software company, and an alum of StubHub, Google and Amazon. 

“I’ve spent my career looking at and driving representation for women in tech,” Singh Cassidy told me this week after joining Serena Williams and private equity investor Larry Tanenbaum in the ownership group of the W’s newest franchise, which will begin playing in 2026. For that reason, she said, becoming a W owner aligned with her values, but it wasn’t the only factor in her decision to invest in sports.

Singh Cassidy had spent the last three years or so considering which league she might put her money into. As an avid hoops fan and Golden State Warriors supporter, she narrowed down her search to professional basketball and ultimately chose the W. “The WNBA just has much more upside,” she said. “Many of these franchises are starting, but the price of entry—and the opportunity as media rights go up—is pretty exponential.”

Singh Cassidy comes to the WNBA  with a range of ideas about how to improve fan experience and maximize ticket value, ones bolstered by her time as StubHub’s president. “And of course, I’m a proud Canadian,” she said. “The Tempo won’t just be Toronto but will be Canada’s team.”

Weekend’s Latest Stories

The Big Read 

Why Sports Leagues Decided to Stop Fighting Influencers and Learn to Love Them

As recently as the last decade, sports leagues looked at fan content as something to stamp out of existence. Back then, they viewed it as pirated material—and a threat to their all-important content deals with broadcast TV networks, which accounted for a major part of their revenues. 

Ohhh, how things change. It’s something of a substantial understatement to say media consumption habits have drastically changed over the past decade, particularly among young people. And as social media creators have increasingly eaten away at traditional sports media, the leagues now see influencers as essential partners, our Sara Germano reports.

When Sara discussed the matter with Bob Carney, the NBA’s senior vice president of digital and social content, he described the league’s strategy as an attempt to establish a “communal viewing” experience. That’s NBA speak for using creators to steer audiences toward live broadcasts and keep the conversation going when the game ends. As he told Sara, the plan is nothing less than the league’s “North Star.”

The Top 5

The Startups Hoping for a ‘MAHA’ Boom

If Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gets his way, what we eat, drink and consume in this country is going to change tremendously. For a widening number of startups, this shift, dubbed “Make America Healthy Again” and led by the Health Department chief, could be a golden opportunity, our Ann Gehan finds. They see the change in government regulations and consumer tastes as a chance to grow sales—and eventually get bought by Big Food, which could decide it’s easier to buy a couple of these startups than develop their own brands in-house.

Power and Influence

Tech Companies Tiptoe Around Trump

It’s not an exaggeration to say things haven’t been going smoothly with the economy since President Donald Trump took office in January, and even though many of the tech elite who threw their support behind him did so for economic reasons, his support in Silicon Valley remains surprisingly intact, according to our Nick Wingfield and Theo Wyatt. 

“I think what’s happening is everybody knows Trump is retaliatory and punitive,” said Adam Kovacevich, CEO of Chamber of Progress, a center-left tech trade organization backed by Amazon, Google and other companies. “And I also think companies learned from the first term that it’s better to use honey with Trump than vinegar. He’s not getting candid feedback from the business community.”

Abram Brown, editor of The Information’s Weekend section, needs to go sort through all his Temu binge orders. Reach him at abe@theinformation.com.

Listening: “SNAFU” (iHeart Radio)

Snafus are awful to live through—but ones that happen to other people generally make for riveting tales. Comedian Ed Helms has been having great fun recounting such chicanery with this podcast for several seasons, and he’s back with a doozy for a third season: a snafu within a snafu, as he puts it. He looks at a forgotten part of Prohibition when the government introduced Formula 6, a toxic chemical additive that made industrial alcohol undrinkable. That move led to devastating consequences and what amounts to “the first modern American culture war,” Helm says.—A.B. 

Reading: “The Golden Road” by William Dalrymple

A strong argument could be made that the 21st century will be India’s century. William Dalrymple would argue such an occurrence wouldn’t be the first time India has reshaped the planet. 

From roughly the third century to the 13th century, India exerted a great amount of cultural and economic influence over a considerable chunk of the developed world (as it existed then), establishing what Dalrymple variously calls the “Indosphere” and “the Golden Road” (hence the title). 

What a marvelous, fascinating realm it was: a domain from which came “not just pioneering merchants, astronomers and astrologers, scientists and mathematicians, doctors and sculptors, but also the holy men, monks and missionaries.” Emanating from those religious figures, Buddhism was perhaps Ancient India’s most widespread export,one promulgated with great enthusiasm by Emperor Ashoka. Ashoka fancied himself an enlightened sort of ruler and ordered Buddhist edicts carved in stone throughout his kingdom; these are some of the earliest surviving Buddhist texts. 

In “The Golden Road,” Dalrymple takes great care to show how we don’t give enough credit to the thinkers and doers of ancient India, who outpaced Western innovation by centuries. Obviously, Ashoka was one, but he was also something of a cautionary tale. As he built his empire, he promised his subjects he’d be available to them “at any time, anywhere.” Meanwhile, he was consistently miserable, historical records show, and perhaps partly because he was an early example of a leader who didn’t know when to log off.—A.B.

Watching: “Étoile” (Amazon Prime)

In the small circle of television auteurs, Amy Sherman-Palladino stands out. Her shows—most famously “Gilmore Girls” and “The Marvellous Mrs. Maisel” are quirky and smart and not about mean, villainous men, which makes her an oddity in this era of television. Her new drama centers on New York City’s premier ballet company as it undertakes a talent swap with its Paris counterpart, hoping to spark publicity and much-needed ticket sales.

Like Sherman-Palladino’s past shows, “Étoile” is colorful and fun to watch, weaving in and out of the dramas around prima donnas both on the stage and in the executive suites of the ballet companies. You don’t have to be a ballet fan to enjoy the extensive dance scenes. To add depth, the series interperses scenes set in Paris and New York, using both English and French in dialogue.

And for Sherman-Palladino fans, there’s the added benefit of cast members from her old series showing up here in new roles. For instance, an aide to the head of the Paris ballet company is played by Yanic Truesdale—“Gilmore Girl” fans will recall his role as a hotel worker in that small-town drama. Similarly, Luke Kirby, who plays one of the lead roles as the head of the New York ballet, was in “Mrs. Maisel” as Lenny Bruce. And while she has had no previous roles in a Sherman-Palladino series, Charlotte Gainsbourg as the head of the French ballet is a delight.—Martin Peers 

Final Thought

The type of “leading indicator” our modern times deserve.

As he built his empire, he promised his subjects he’d be available to them “at any time, anywhere.” Meanwhile, he was consistently miserable, historical records show, and perhaps partly because he was an early example of a leader who didn’t know when to log off.—A.B. Watching: “Étoile” (Amazon Prime) In the small circle of television auteurs, Amy Sherman-Palladino stands out. Her shows—most famously “Gilmore Girls” and “The Marvellous Mrs. Maisel” are quirky and smart and not about mean, villainous men, which makes her an oddity in this era of television. Her new drama centers on New York City’s premier ballet company as it undertakes a talent swap with its Paris counterpart, hoping to spark publicity and much-needed ticket sales. Like Sherman-Palladino’s past shows, “Étoile” is colorful and fun to watch, weaving in and out of the dramas around prima donnas both on the stage and in the executive suites of the ballet companies. You don’t have to be a ballet fan to enjoy the extensive dance scenes. To add depth, the series interperses scenes set in Paris and New York, using both English and French in dialogue. And for Sherman-Palladino fans, there’s the added benefit of cast members from her old series showing up here in new roles. For instance, an aide to the head of the Paris ballet company is played by Yanic Truesdale—“Gilmore Girl” fans will recall his role as a hotel worker in that small-town drama. Similarly, Luke Kirby, who plays one of the lead roles as the head of the New York ballet, was in “Mrs. Maisel” as Lenny Bruce. And while she has had no previous roles in a Sherman-Palladino series, Charlotte Gainsbourg as the head of the French ballet is a delight.—Martin Peers The type of “leading indicator” our modern times deserve. title: The Startups Hoping for a ‘MAHA’ Boom
feed_content:
A few weeks ago, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. Health and Human Services secretary, and Marty Makary, the new Food and Drug Administration commissioner, announced plans to ban eight commonly used petroleum-based dyes from food products in the U.S. Kennedy envisions far more changes ahead in his crusade to force American food companies to change, including removing items like soda and candy from SNAP benefits and revamping the approval process for new food ingredients.

If even only a small portion of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” agenda comes to fruition, what appears on our plates could change pretty dramatically. The wave of change stands to put enormous pressure on existing food and beverage conglomerates like PepsiCo and Coca-Cola to quickly alter their businesses.

But Kennedy’s plans also present a moment of fertile opportunity for a swath of startups that have already been trying to capitalize on consumers’ growing focus on ingredients and health—and five of the most significant ones are highlighted below. For these companies, a MAHA boom would be a golden age.
full_content: A few weeksago, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. Health and Human Services secretary, and Marty Makary, the new Food and Drug Administration commissioner, announced plans to ban eight commonly used petroleum-based dyes from food products in the U.S. Kennedy envisions far more changes ahead in his crusade to force American food companies to change, including removing items like soda and candy from SNAP benefits and revamping the approval process for new food ingredients. If even only a small portion of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” agenda comes to fruition, what appears on our plates could change pretty dramatically. The wave of change stands to put enormous pressure on existing food and beverage conglomerates like PepsiCo and Coca-Cola to quickly alter their businesses. But Kennedy’s plans also present a moment of fertile opportunity for a swath of startups that have already been trying to capitalize on consumers’ growing focus on ingredients and health—and five of the most significant ones are highlighted below. For these companies, a MAHA boom would be a golden age. “The consumer now is just getting more and more granular” with what they’re looking for at the grocery store, said Kevin McCray, co-founder of Wild Fox Foods, a line of seed oil free nut mixes and protein bars founded earlier this year. McCray previously co-founded and ran Kevin’s Natural Foods, a line of paleo- and keto-friendly entrees and sauces that grew to nearly $200 million in annual revenue before Mars bought it in 2023 for roughly $800 million. Wild Fox and other startups are cropping up to cater to new shopper demands like products free of seed oils and dyes, and some more-established brands are getting a boost as well. Around 40% of Americans say they’re aware of the MAHA movement, according to asurveyby The New Consumer and Coefficient Capital earlier this year. And the top food-related concern of surveyed shoppers was processed and ultraprocessed foods, a key target of MAHA, ahead of contamination like E. coli and salmonella, pesticides and genetically modified organisms. Even with Kennedy leading the charge on MAHA, most brands insist they’re not trying to get political. “MAHA obviously has a political brand on it, but I think the core question of should we make it easier for everyone to be healthy is a pretty agreeable bipartisan issue,” insisted Seth Goldstein, a co-founder of Ancient Crunch, a seed oil free chip company. Either way, startups are one of the best ways to try to change the world of food, particularly if big conglomerates acquire them, said investor Jason Karp, who has backed seed oil free restaurant chain True Food Kitchen and previously founded Hu Chocolate. “If Pepsi changed the formulation of Siete, they would get crucified,” he said. (PepsiCo said late last year it would acquire Siete Foods for $1.2 billion.) “The companies are very aware they cannot change the ingredients without very visibly doing so.”  ForJesse and Ben’s, a line of frozen french fries that launched in stores earlier this year, the MAHA wave has sparked a wave of inbound interest from retailers, potential investors and shoppers, said co-founder Jesse Konig. Konig’s fries, which are made with avocado oil and beef tallow rather than the typical canola oil, recently launched nationwide at Sprouts and is planning a national rollout at Whole Foods at the end of the month. Konig, a longtime food truck and restaurant owner in the Washington area, says he first started hearing more “grumblings” about ultraprocessed foods and seed oils in 2022. It reminded him of the early days when he had a food truck, and he and his business partner were researching beef suppliers and struggling to find high-quality vendors. “We got a lot of weird answers about ‘This is the way things are done in food.’ And we didn’t feel satisfied with that, so we started doing a lot of our own research—we read “The Omnivore’s Dilemma,” we watched “Food Inc.,” trying to understand all the stuff in the background of the food industry,” he said. Konig said when talking with retail buyers, he compares Jesse & Ben’s to more-established brands like Siete Foods and Boulder Canyon, a chip brand owned by snack giant Utz. Those companies have found mainstream success by emphasizing better ingredients like avocado oil. And while the Trump administration has a “perspective” on food, Konig insists the brand wants to avoid politics. “We’ve tried to stay very much like, ‘These are french fries, everyone loves fries. What is the product that we’d be happy to feed our friends and family?’” Kevin McCray,Wild Fox’s co-founder, says he was into no seed oils and no dyes “before it was cool.” After focusing on dinner and larger meals with the development and growth of Kevin’s Natural Foods, McCray and his co-founders are now turning their attention to snacks with Wild Fox Foods. The team zeroed in on nuts and trail mix as a good starting point for a healthy snack brand, but McCray said he was surprised by the number of products in the category that were still full of additives, seed oils and artificial ingredients. The brand is planning its first retail launches for this summer, McCray said. Despite Washington’s newfound interest in stamping out seed oils, McCray said he views them as less of a political siren call and more of a simple indicator that can help shoppers steer clear of processed foods. “They’re a good bogeyman for highly processed foods,” McCray said of seed oils. “A lot of the time, if you see a common seed oil, you should just make sure that that food hasn’t been highly processed.”  Kettle & Fire, which sells bone broths and soups, was founded in 2015 by brothers Justin and Nick Mares. The brand has hit its stride recently—it raised $43 million from investors including Colter Ventures late last year, in a deal that bought out some of its early backers and valued it at $200 million. Growing shopper interest in high-protein and seed oil free foods has given Kettle & Fire a boost recently, doubling sales to more than $100 million last year. The brand emphasizes its focus on nutrient-dense products and more collagen, amino acids, and vitamins and minerals compared to other soups and broths, which often rely on powdered formulations or added flavors. Justin Mares remains chair of Kettle & Fire’s board but has jumped into other MAHA endeavors: In mid-2022, he co-founded Truemed, a startup that helps users spend health savings account funds on fitness gear and supplements, with tech entrepreneur Calley Means, now a White House special government employee working closely with Kennedy on food policy. Some brands have leaned more into courting controversy. Steven Rofrano, one ofAncient Crunch’s co-founders, has appeared on podcasts popular with right-leaning audiences, like conservative influencer Alex Clark’s health and wellness-focused “Culture Apothecary.” And the company’s Masa Chips brand has been promoted by Gary Brecka, a health and wellness influencer who has spoken out against what he says are the dangers of adding fluoride to drinking water. “Our mission is to make default healthy snacks available,” Goldstein said. “We do our best, generally speaking, to make sure that we are not taking sides on things that are more controversial,” he added. Ancient Crunch fries its tortilla and potato chips in beef tallow. The brand doesn’t use other avocado oil or olive oil because of concerns about dilution with canola oil or other additives, Goldstein said. But there aren’t many affordable facilities set up for commercial production with beef tallow in the U.S., he said, which means the company has to handle all of its production itself. That’s an uncommon step for young food brands, which typically rely on outsourced production. So Ancient Crunch, which Goldstein said has raised roughly $10 million from investors so far, is also in talks with investors to secure funding for a new factory, he added. The new facility would help the company increase production so it can stock national retailers and reduce prices: A four-pack of Masa Chips’ 5-ounce bags currently retails for $52. And in addition to making products for its own brands, Ancient Crunch is exploring ways to supply tallow to fast-food and quick-service restaurants, Goldstein said, a gap in the market left when McDonald’s stopped frying its french fries in beef tallow in 1990.  Colostrum is one of the dietary supplements most in vogue thanks to MAHA. The supplement, which advocates claim can help with everything from gut health to boosting immunity, has quickly become popular with wellness-focused influencers who tout it online, andArmrais one of the biggest brands to popularize it. Armra launched sales in 2021 and quickly grew to $120 million in annual revenue by 2023. The brand has mostly relied on online sales so far, but more recently, it’s been making a push into bricks-and-mortar retail, launching nationwide at Sprouts late last year. Founder Sarah Rahal, a neurologist by training, initially bootstrapped the brand, but Armra has raised nearly $9 million from investors, according to PitchBook. Armra is facing more competition lately. Influencer Alex Clark promotes Cowboy Colostrum, a competing brand, on her “Culture Apothecary” podcast, and popular tradwife influencer Hannah Neeleman, who’s known online as Ballerina Farm, highlights colostrum as an ingredient in her brand’s protein powder, also called Ballerina Farm. Otherbig supplement brandsare launching their own colostrum products as well, including a powder from Bloom Nutrition that came out in November. title: Tech Companies Tiptoe Around Trump
feed_content:
On Thursday, Microsoft announced it had jacked up the prices on its game products, raising the price of its flagship Xbox console by $100—or 20%—to $600. It was an extraordinary move: Five-year-old consoles like the current generation of Xboxes almost always see price cuts, not increases.

To anyone even dimly aware of economic news, it was fairly obvious Microsoft’s Xbox changes were a reaction to the Trump administration’s tariffs on electronics manufactured overseas. But that wasn’t clear from the company’s anodyne explanation for the change, which said the increase was prompted by “market conditions and the rising cost of development.”
full_content: On Thursday, Microsoftannounced it had jacked up the prices on its game products, raising the price of its flagship Xbox console by $100—or 20%—to $600. It was an extraordinary move: Five-year-old consoles like the current generation of Xboxes almost always see price cuts, not increases. To anyone even dimly aware of economic news, it was fairly obvious Microsoft’s Xbox changes were a reaction to the Trump administration’s tariffs on electronics manufactured overseas. But that wasn’t clearfrom the company’s anodyne explanationfor the change, which said the increase was prompted by “market conditions and the rising cost of development.” More than 100 days into the presidency of Donald Trump, the tech leaders and companies who welcomed his second term don’t seem to have had changes of heart—at least not ones they’ll admit to publicly. The most full-throated Trump backers in tech still believe he can unleash American dynamism in artificial intelligence, crypto, manufacturing and other areas. And tech companies like Microsoft are going out of their way to avoid crossing the president by, for example, attributing their price increases to his tariffs. “I think what’s happening is everybody knows Trump is retaliatory and punitive,” said Adam Kovacevich, CEO of Chamber of Progress, a center-left tech trade organization backed by Amazon, Google and other companies. “And I also think companies learned from the first term that it’s better to use honey with Trump than vinegar. He’s not getting candid feedback from the business community.” It’s easy to understand why Microsoft chose not to telegraph the impact of the administration’s tariffs too explicitly to consumers. Earlier in the week, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt blasted Amazon for what she called a “a hostile and political act” after Punchbowl Newsreported that the retailerwas considering showing the impact of tariffs on prices on its site. Amazon subsequently said it had considered such a plan for Haul, an Amazon site that sells inexpensive Chinese-made goods, but dropped the idea before the White House’s response. When Amazon CEO Andy Jassy addressed Trump’s tariffs on this Thursday evening’s earnings call, it almost sounded like he was discussing a severe weather event rather than a political decision. “It’s hard to tell what’s going to happen with tariffs right now,” Jassy said. “It’s hard to tell where they’re going to settle and when they’re going to settle.” Big tech companies have much to lose from provoking the president. Nearly all of them are the subjects of federal antitrust cases or investigations that could force radical changes on them, not to mention regulations that could help or hurt their businesses in AI, cryptocurrency and social media, among many other areas. And while many of the largest tech companies and its leaders have sought to curry favor with the president—for example, by donating $1 million each to his inauguration—Trump isn’t going to let up on them, said Mike Davis, a pugnacious Trump supporter who runs a right-wing advocacy group, the Article III Project. Shortly before the Federal Trade Commission’s antitrust trial against Meta Platforms began last month, Davis said he reminded Trump in the Oval Office about how Facebook had removed him from its platform in 2020. Davis said that reminder helped squash Meta’s hopes of reaching a pre-trial settlement with the government. “These big tech platforms censored, silenced, deplatformed and canceled conservatives including President Trump,” said Davis. “Spending $1 million on the inauguration after President Trump won in 2024 is not going to make up for that.” There’s little sign that the most prominent pro-Trump techies are having second thoughts about the president. Earlier this week, at the Hill and Valley Forum in Washington, onstage comments from many tech and political leaders included effusive praise of Trump. “We have the best leader in the world. President Trump is objectively and truly a sample of one. No one who loves this country is [as] relentless and as resilient, and the only person able to inspire a golden age. The stars have aligned,” said Jacob Helberg, an organizer of the conference. Helberg is an adviser to Palantir’s CEO and the Trump administration’s nominee for undersecretary of state for economic growth, energy and the environment. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whom Helberg interviewed at the conference, could have used his time onstage to complain about export controls on semiconductors, which Joe Biden’s administration put into place and Trump’s has tightened even more. Those controls forced Nvidia to take a $5.5 billion write-down on lost China sales in April and to startredesigning a key AI chip. Instead, Huang praised Trump: “I’m delighted that the administration is really encouraging and supporting the industry to onshore manufacturing,” he said. One of the few pro-Trump tech investors who has been willing to express his disagreements with the administration is Joe Lonsdale, a Palantir co-founder and venture capitalist at 8VC. Through his outspoken Twitter account, Lonsdale has criticized the president’s plan for acrypto national reserve, his opposition toport automationand some of histariffs. He has evenquestioned the wisdomof needling political moderates, as Elon Musk and Eric Trump have, by promoting the idea of Donald Trump running for a third term in 2028 (the U.S. Constitution prohibits such a run). Lonsdale didn’t respond to a request for comment. Still, for some Trump supporters in tech, the trade war has ruptured their faith in a president they believed would be more pro-business than his political rival, Kamala Harris. Craig Fuller, founder and CEO of the 8VC-backed supply chain data and media startup FreightWaves, said he had backed the president because he believed Trump would take a measured approach to combating some of the discrepancies in global trade. By Valentine’s Day, however, Fuller realized that Trump was going to be more disruptive and extreme than he’d hoped. “We had this massive acceleration in tariffs on Canada and Mexico, and you had that conversation about [the] 51st state and all that nonsense,” Fuller said. “That was when we saw material weakening in freight.” Trump’s announcements of a wide array of new tariffs on April 2—at an event the White House dubbed Liberation Day—didn’t make Fuller any more confident about Trump’s handling of trade. “I was hoping we’d get some certainty and logic to the policies, but it was clear this thing was going off the rails,” he said of the event. In the near term, the tariffs have been good for Fuller’s business because demand for supply chain data and news spikes during chaotic periods, Fuller said. But many leaders in the supply chain industry have told Fuller they’ve paused orders and expect to cut staff within the next one to two months if Trump doesn’t back off from his tariffs. At a recent meeting Fuller attended with several manufacturing executives and Republican members of Congress, the mood was tense. “There was a sense of betrayal, where you were supposed to deliver growth for us and what they were getting was quite the opposite,” Fuller said. Still, Fuller added, he isn’t sure whether he regrets supporting Trump because he feels Harris didn’t adequately explain her vision for the economy. While big tech companies are largely refraining from criticizing Trump directly—and tiptoeing around the subject of tariffs—there are signs some of them are willing to risk his displeasure. Earlier this week, The New York Timesreported that Microsoft had droppedseveral attorneys from the law firm Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, who were representing the company in a case involving its acquisition of Activision Blizzard. The firm was among several top law firms that recently struck deals to do pro bono work for causes supported by Trump in an effort to avoid punitive actions by the administration. In place of the Simpson attorneys, Microsoft retained lawyers from Jenner & Block, a firm that ismounting a court challengeto a Trump administration executive order that targeted its ability to work for federal government clients. title: Anthropic to Buy Back Employee Shares at $61.5 Billion Valuation
feed_content:
Anthropic is offering to buy back shares from hundreds of current and former employees, the first transaction of its kind for the four-year-old company. The buyback is a sign of how integral these have become in rewarding employees at fast-growing startups and retaining rare research talent in the artificial intelligence talent war.

San Francisco–based Anthropic is allowing current and former employees who worked for the company for at least two years to sell up to 20% of their equity, with a maximum of $2 million each, the person said. The buyback values the AI startup at $61.5 billion, the same valuation as in its March fundraising, according to a person familiar with the transaction, which could amount to hundreds of millions of dollars.

The buyback is a sign of how integral these have become in rewarding employees at fast-growing startups and retaining rare research talent in the artificial intelligence talent war. San Francisco–based Anthropic is allowing current and former employees who worked for the company for at least two years to sell up to 20% of their equity, with a maximum of $2 million each, the person said. The buyback values the AI startup at $61.5 billion, the same valuation as in its March fundraising, according to a person familiar with the transaction, which could amount to hundreds of millions of dollars. The buyback should be finalized by the end of the month, the person said. The company, founded by former OpenAI researchers, currently employs more than 800 people, up fromabout 300 at the end of 2023. Large secondaries have become commonplace among startups nearing the decade mark, which is around the time many have historically gone public. OpenAI, now nearly a decade old, has allowed employees and ex-employees to collectively sell about $2.7 billion worth of shares in the past few years. Last year, design companyFigmaand enterprise software firmDatabrickssimilarly allowed some employees to sell hundreds of millions’ worth of shares. Not every startup allows former employees to cash in their stock. Data-labeling firm Scale AI, which is close to finalizing a $150 million share sale valuing it at around $25 billion, isexcluding ex-employees from the transaction. While many of those startups have arranged sales of employee stock to investors, profitable startupsByteDanceandStripehave bought back employee shares. This strategy can limit the number of new investors in a company and involves less work than a share sale. Anthropic is still burning cash. But it has just raised $3.5 billion in capital led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, bringing its total raised to more than $15 billion. The latest valuation is equivalent to $56.09 per share, according to a filing. In March, Anthropicpassed$1.4 billion in annualized revenue, implying monthly revenue of around $116 million. That was up about 40% from the $1 billion in annualized revenue Anthropic hit at the end of 2024. Stephanie Palazzolo is a reporter at The Information covering artificial intelligence. This is the latest sign that large companies are looking to tap into the surging interest from developers in AI-powered coding tools, which has been stoked by startups Anysphere, which makes Cursor, and Windsurf. title: Endowments Need Cash, but VC Firms Have None to Offer
feed_content:
The long and fruitful relationship between venture capital firms and university endowments is facing hard times as both sides struggle with worsening cash squeezes.

Over the past three years, VC funds have been returning money to their investors at the lowest rates in the past 25 years, levels that have only occurred during major market and economic downturns.
full_content: The long andfruitful relationship between venture capital firms and university endowments is facing hard times as both sides struggle with worsening cash squeezes. Over the past three years, VC funds have been returning money to their investors at the lowest rates in the past 25 years, levels that have only occurred during major market and economic downturns. “From a VC perspective, we’re just not getting any liquidity there,” said John Lawrence, chief investment officer of Rice University’s $8.1 billion endowment. At the same time, endowments need cash more than ever. They are facing a major onslaught from the Donald Trump administration, which is cutting schools’ funding and threatening to hit them with higher taxes. Rice’s endowment is sitting on more cash than normal, after getting payouts from some of its investments. But Lawrence has been slow to invest it because of uncertainty in the markets. None of the endowment’s core VC managers are currently fundraising, he said. The impact on tech startups could be felt for years into the future as the flow of cash slows and pressure on companies to go public or merge increases. Over the past three years, VC and growth equity funds have returned an average of 8.2% of their assets to investors, according to data from Hamilton Lane, a consultant and asset manager. That’s far below the average of 18.2% since 2000 and just below the levels hit during the burst of the tech bubble in the early 2000s and the financial crisis late in that decade.  The slump is especially tough on endowments, some of the earliest and most consistent backers of VC funds. Endowments rely on cash returns to help fund university operations. Without money flowing back from VC funds, they are having to find it elsewhere and struggling to justify making new investments. The endowments are getting more cash from their private equity investments, which have returned more than VC funds have in each of the past four years, according to Hamilton Lane data. But neither group has made above-average distributions since 2021, when giddy public markets provided an off-ramp for investors to sell stakes in dozens of companies. Private tech companies have recently been avoiding public markets, cutting off that source of cash. As a result, most endowments are already at or above their targeted allocations to VC managers. “I don’t hear too many of those long-term endowments saying we’re underallocated at the moment,” said Tim Yates, who oversees more than $15 billion of assets from nonprofits at investment manager Commonfund. Endowments are under pressure to increase payouts to cover funding gaps after the federal government pulled grants to Harvard and other elite universities the president has accused of fostering antisemitism and ideological bias. Republicans in Congresshave proposed taxing endowments at 21%, in line with the corporate rate. Endowments now have a tax rate of 1.4%. On Friday, Trump threatened on social media to revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status. President Donald Trump’s decision to raise tariffs on U.S. trading partners last month has also dealt a blow to endowments’ public investments, such as stocks and bonds, as well as its VC and private equity holdings. Major endowments sold private equity fund stakes at steep discounts during the 2008 financial crisis to cover losses in their public stock holdings. Under normal circumstances, most endowments can weather market downturns, but the combination of factors hitting them right now is making that difficult. “This is the type of thing endowments are supposed to be resilient against,” said Roger Vincent, a former officer at the Cornell University endowment, who runs Summation Capital, a private equity fund investor. Endowments are turning to secondary markets to sell stakes in private equity and VC funds instead of waiting for cash to flow back. Yale University’s $41.4 billion endowment is working with Evercore to sell a multibillion-dollar portfolio of private equity fund managers, the first secondary sale in its history. Harvard University’s $53.2 billion endowment is also looking to sell a nearly $1 billion chunk of its private equity portfolio, said one person familiar with the process. Secondaries Investor earlier reported on Yale’s potential sale, and Bloomberg first reported on Harvard’s. Sequoia Capital, whose investors include Notre Dame University’s endowment,has devised its own solutionto the cash crunch facing endowments. The firm last year purchased from its own investors $861 million worth of shares in payments company Stripe at a $70 billion valuation, returning cash to the investors. Sequoia in 2021 createda new fund structurethat gave it the license to hold investments indefinitely, citing companies like Block that continued to appreciate in public markets. A raft of new funds has also emerged to buy secondary stakes in private equity and VC funds from investors such as endowments. On Thursday, private equity firm Apollo Global Management said it had raised $5.4 billion for such a fund, exceeding its target. Both the companies that are dependent on VC funding and the VC managers themselves are turning to other sources of capital to make up for the drought in endowment cash. OpenAI tapped Japan’s SoftBank to lead a $40 billion funding round it announced in March. VC managers arealso widening their base of investorsto include more pensions and sovereign wealth funds. The liquidity squeeze and secondary sales could signal a decline in the long-term strategy for endowments. Under former endowment chief David Swensen, Yale pioneered a strategy that leaned heavily on external VC and private equity managers, which have managed as muchas 41% of the endowment’s assetsin recent years. Swensen’s approach paid off handsomely,netting the endowment 13.7% annual gainsduring his tenure from 1985 to 2021. Its wider adoption at other endowments helped fuel the growth of private equity and VC managers such as Blackstone and Andreessen Horowitz.But Yale’s returns have faltered recently. Both Harvard and Yale began preparing for their portfolio sales last year, months before the Trump administration began targeting universities and sending markets into turmoil, said people familiar with the decisions.

title: DOJ’s Google Data Sharing Proposal was Based on Google-Yahoo Japan Deal
feed_content:
The Justice Department’s proposal that Google be forced to share its search data with rivals in order to restore search engine competition used a 2010 deal Google struck with Yahoo Japan as the “foundation” for the proposal, a lawyer for the DOJ said in court on Friday.

Google has argued that ...
full_content: The Justice Department’sproposal that Google be forced to share its search data with rivals in order to restore search engine competition used a 2010 deal Google struck with Yahoo Japan as the “foundation” for the proposal, a lawyer for the DOJ said in court on Friday. Google has argued that the Department of Justice’s data sharing proposal would create privacy concerns and make it “unviable” for Google to continue investing in research and development at the same rate. The Yahoo Japan agreement included some search index data similar to what plaintiffs are requesting and required Google to provide some search features to Yahoo Japan, according to documents shown in court and testimony from a Google director of product management, Jesse Adkins. However, the search index data shared with Yahoo Japan was for Google’s Japanese search index, not its global search index, and the agreement was later amended to share less data, Adkins testified. The agreement also restricted how Yahoo Japan could use the data to protect Google’s “trade secrets,” Adkins said, restrictions that do not occur in the plaintiffs’ proposed final judgement.

title: How Sports Leagues Learned to Love Creators Instead of Fighting Them
feed_content:
In summer 2021, Matt Scharf and some of his guy friends were playing a round of golf at a leafy course near Austin, Texas, when they arrived at the 14th hole, a 290-yard uphill par 4. Clad in a busy Hawaiian-print polo and a trucker hat, Scharf thwacked a drive straight down the fairway to the green, eliciting immediate whoops of “Dude!” and “Bro!” from his companions. A few moments later, as if on time delay, his friends who were already on the green went berserk: Scharf had hit an improbable hole in one.

These were not merely buddies out for a casual afternoon, but emerging social media creators hard at work. Scharf and his 20-something pals filmed this exact scene from three handheld cameras for their YouTube channel, Good Good Golf, where this video, “The Greatest Golf Shot in YouTube History,” has since racked up more than 5 million views and still ranks as the channel’s second most popular clip ever. It helped launch Good Good Golf’s rise to digital stardom, and the channel now has nearly 2 million subscribers, a crowd drawn to the guys’ youthful enthusiasm and their ease with speaking directly to the camera, inviting viewers onto the course with them.

Their content has caught the attention of traditional broadcasters like NBC’s Golf Channel, which struck up a partnership in 2023 with Good Good to stage tournaments they can cross-promote and broadcast on both their platforms.

“We do think there’s a place for us to learn from YouTube content creators,” said Tom Knapp, NBC’s executive vice president of golf. Knapp thinks they can help him solve a problem that has nagged at him for 25 years: a need to lure in younger viewers. He wants to blend the core Golf Channel audience of Wall Street executives and Washington power brokers with YouTube’s “golf bros” (his words). After all, they all share the same underlying passion: golf. “There’s no reason why we can’t serve both masters,” he said.

After all, they all share the same underlying passion: golf. “There’s no reason why we can’t serve both masters,” he said. The Arena is a new franchise within Weekend that covers the business and future of sports.Read moreof its coverage fromThe Information’s Sara Germano. The collaboration between Good Good and the Golf Channel highlights one of the most important emerging trends in the sports industry today: the pairing of young influencers and established leagues and broadcasters. It’s a kind of symbiosis: Legacy media and professional sports leagues lend credibility to social media stars. Meanwhile, the sports establishment is tapping creators like the Good Good crew in hopes that they can deliver the elusive audience of young, fervently engaged viewers. The union of influencers and the sports industry is a stark shift from their relationship in the past. As recently as the 2010s, sports executives were aggressively policing social media to take down game highlights, hoping to protect broadcast TV partners who paid billions of dollars for content that other people were sharing online without paying anything. But cable TV has precipitously declined over the past 15 years, while young people’s habits have greatly morphed. Today more than two-thirds of viewers under age 35 say they scroll social media while watching live sports, and fewer than 20% watch an entire game from start to finish, according to a 2024 survey from PwC. So the leagues are evolving, too. And rather than fighting against influencers and fan content, the leagues are seeing them as essential partners. As a result, content creators hold an important role in the new sports ecosystem: They keep distracted young viewers engaged and  continue the conversation around the still-crucial broadcasts of live games. “Sports obviously is still very powerful and has an opportunity to aggregate audiences into a live window,” said Jon Cruz, global head of sports partnerships at YouTube. “But I think league commissioners and decision-makers understand that in order to meet the needs of younger fans today, they’re going to have to be in a number of places.” Exactly how these leagues, broadcasters and creators can best work together is still largely unproven. Leagues ultimately have one goal: to command high ratings, regardless of where their games are aired. And it is still too early to determine whether influencers can be relied upon to consistently funnel young viewership to live sports. At the same time, influencers are third parties working on social platforms, and sharing licensed sports content with them can risk distorting the league’s core brand or messaging. Nearly every league has shifted toward embracing influencers, though the exact dimensions of their plans vary to some degree. That’s bringing yet another profound wave of transformation in how sports are presented to the world. The NBA All-StarWeekend is a showcase of the league’s most talented players, giving the likes of LeBron James and Stephen Curry an exhibition game midway through the season to celebrate their accomplishments. But to anyonein the San Francisco Bay Areathis past February, where the league held its annual festivities for 2025, the All-Star Weekend equally showcased the creator set. TikToker Khaby Lame, Twitch streamer Kai Cenat and Instagram comedian Druski participated in the All-Star Celebrity Game, while YouTuber Jesser served as a judge in the dunk contest. The culmination of the weekend was the Sunday evening halftime show featuring MrBeast, who hosted one of his trademark skills challenges complete with a cash prize: A fan from the crowd won $100,000 for successfully sinking a half-court shot. The stunt generated 165 million views across social media. As a league spokesperson described it, the weekend represented “the culmination of a decade of work” by the NBA to incorporate creators into its media ecosystem. The league formally established a creator program in 2016 to collaborate with streamers, Instagrammers, tweeters and, eventually, TikTokers. This year the roster includes more than 150 such creators, who share their own takes on pro basketball. Bob Carney, the NBA’s senior vice president of digital and social content, described the league’s focus on a “communal viewing experience,” where creators keep fans inundated with NBA content and direct them to tune into live games. That approach ensures the conversation around basketball keeps humming. “It’s so clear to us that that’s the North Star,” he said. The NBA’s creator strategy is heavily predicated on the league’s new $76 billion domestic broadcast package with ESPN, NBC and Amazon Prime Video, each of which will air games beginning this fall on their networks and streaming platforms. The NBA already works with creators to encourage social media viewers to tune into live games, but to date that has largely meant trying to convince people to put down their phones and pick up a remote to turn on the television. By contrast, streaming platforms offer less friction when it comes to switching between TikTok and live games, since users can access both from within the same device, effectively putting the games one click away. A direct illustration of the strategy, which uses social media to direct viewers to legacy broadcasts, is the burgeoning partnership between Good Good Golf and NBC. In February 2024, they co-developed and staged a tournament for influencers and celebrities like football quarterback Johnny Manziel called the Good Good Desert Open. The first 75 minutes of coverage appeared on the Good Good YouTube channel before viewers were prompted to switch over to Peacock for the event’s conclusion. Knapp and the team at NBC anticipated that maybe one in four viewers might migrate from YouTube to Peacock. To their shock, more than 60% converted. “We had a live event on our air that was the youngest event in the history of the Golf Channel by 20 years,” Knapp said. “Twenty years in TV is gigantic.” As a result, Knapp started getting calls from categories of advertising partners he’d never worked with before, like soft drinks and fitness apparel brands. The Good Good relationship “opens up an entire new category for us.” (They renewed the Desert Open for 2025 with similar results and plan to continue such programming quarterly.) It happens to be just as beneficial for the creators themselves: In March, Good Good secured a $45 million funding round from Peyton Manning’s Omaha Productions, Manhattan West Private Equity and others. “The whole golf world probably saw that we were onto something,” said Matt Kendrick, CEO of Good Good Golf. He co-founded the group during the pandemic by teaming up with skilled shot makers like Scharf to make “golf entertainment.” Their videos are as much about inviting viewers along for a fun afternoon on the golf course as they are about providing a platform for selling apparel and merchandise, like the fluorescent Hawaiian polo and trucker hat Scharf wore in his hole-in-one highlight. “People feel like this is a part of their lives. They come home and they watch Good Good. They engage and they start attaching themselves to certain characters that are part of Good Good, and they feel like they really know them,” Kendrick told me. “You’re just never going to get that from a traditional golf broadcast.” While creators andthe sports industry enjoy a productive working relationship today, it wasn’t always this way. As recently as the 2010s, many leagues took a hard-line approach against individual fans sharing their content online, enlisting cybersecurity firms to monitor social media for illegal use of sports intellectual property and delete it from the internet. The rationale was fairly straightforward: Giant media conglomerates like Disney and Paramount paid billions of dollars for the exclusive rights to air games and wanted to reserve all of the traffic and viewership for themselves. As the rights holders, the leagues policed illegal sharing. Over the last five years or so, sports have altered course and greatly softened their crackdown on sharing game highlights, industry executives told me. Perhaps nothing better illustrates the shift than the evolution of Eyal Arad’s Tel Aviv, Israel–based company, Videocites. Arad originally co-founded Videocites in 2014 to combat internet piracy and has worked with each of the big four U.S. sports leagues to monitor their intellectual property. In recent years, though, Videocites’ work has shifted dramatically toward measuring fan engagement and helping leagues and other brands identify who is sharing their content. Using Videocites gives a league’s front office a more robust picture of all the people discussing its sport, and it then has a list of creators it can choose to partner with or market to. “The difference between piracy and fan engagement is basically your policy,” Arad told me. For the leagues, “we track everything you have on social media, everything people create around you. If it’s legitimate, we would measure it, help you monetize and grow it. If it’s illegal, we help you take it down as soon as possible.” As a result, Videocites’ fan engagement services have swelled from basically nonexistent five years ago to 70% of its revenues today, Arad said, while attitudes toward what constitutes piracy have evolved “Everyone sitting in the audience is posting something on their Instagram, and then all of a sudden you would take down their content? That’s so aggressive that you would lose your audience,” he said. “That’s how people engage today: They post a photo of themselves at the game.” While not every fan who posts a selfie at a Warriors game is an influencer or a pirate, it certainly helps that leagues like the NBA now see social media as additive to their bottom line rather than an infringement on their media partners. Carney told me the league uses Videocites to identify creators in every part of the world, even those who don’t necessarily have huge followings yet, as possible collaborators. And the NBA gives those creators it selects for its program login access to more than 10 years of league highlights, which they can use to develop Reels for Instagram and TikTok mashups. “If you’re creating high-quality, engaging storytelling content around the NBA every day, then we’re obviously interested in bringing you into our network,” Carney said. Another reason established leagues came to embrace creators is their potential for engagement overseas. When the NFL played its first regular season game in Brazil last fall, executives opted to do the once unthinkable and allow a popular local YouTuber, Casimiro Miguel, to livestream the Eagles-Packers matchup in São Paulo from his channel, CazéTV. Without fixed broadcast agreements in certain global markets, the NFL is free to experiment with different local strategies, which in the case of the Brazil game also included distribution on traditional networks RedeTV! and ESPN Brazil. “The rights in different countries are not as robust as they are here in the U.S.,” said Ian Trombetta, senior vice president of social, influencer and content marketing for the NFL. That opens up the opportunity to work with a YouTuber like CazéTV who “can put a different lens on the game” for local fans, who are less familiar with a uniquely American sport. Within niche sports,creators aren’t merely amplifying the conversation but playing a starring role for startup leagues. Tiara Williams should have been enjoying her senior year at Texas Tech when the world went into lockdown in 2020. A collegiate track-and-field athlete, she missed her final season to compete in the heptathlon, the same sprinting, jumping, and throwing multievent that once made Jackie Joyner-Kersee a superstar. To fill the downtime, Williams started going on Instagram live, inviting fellow athletes to come hang out with her online, which is where she realized she had a knack for getting track stars to open up and be vulnerable on camera. Eventually, she enrolled in a training program for track-and-field storytellers run by existing journalists in the sport who wanted to diversify its media coverage. To hone her interview skills, Williams began attending elite meets, culminating with summer 2023, when she decided to spend $6,000 on flights and accommodations to cover the World Athletics Championships in Hungary. There she scored one-on-ones with many of the best runners on the planet. “I call it the Budapest bomb,” said Williams, who has more than 70,000 followers across Instagram, X, YouTube and TikTok as @_realtalkwithtee. “It blew up my career.” Her fans seem to appreciate her conversational style: While many track journalists shove a microphone at an out-of-breath sprinter and demand they “tell us about your race,” Williams handed them a minifan to cool down, complimented their nails and allowed the interview to unfurl naturally. “There’s never a time where I’m trying to navigate a certain story out of them,” Williams said. “It’s more like, ‘What’s on your mind?’ ‘How do you feel?’ And the hard conversations naturally come out when the athlete is comfortable.” In Hungary, Williams’ approach paid off early in the meet when defending men’s 100 meter champion Fred Kerley of the U.S. failed to advance out of the semi-finals—a shocking development that left traditional media stunned. Having developed a rapport with Williams through her presence at other meets, hestopped onlyto talk with her. The resulting interview caught the eye of Michael Johnson, a four-time Olympic champion sprinter whose double gold medals at the 1996 Atlanta Games made him a global icon. As it happened, Johnson was in Budapest working on a new business venture within track and field. He saw Williams’ Instagram chats as a refreshing new point of view for one of the oldest sports on the planet. “I just kept seeing these athletes and how I was seeing a different side of the athlete when they talk to Tee versus when they would do some mainstream interview,” Johnson told me. The two ended up having lunch in Budapest where they compared notes on how to innovate within the sport. That led Johnson to hire Williams to promote his project, a new series of elite meets called Grand Slam Track, debuting this spring. After his time as an Olympian and later as a BBC commentator, Johnson felt he understood how traditional media covered his sport—and he found it dull. Reporters would “build your story, go interview the subject, and just kind of fill in the blanks,” he told me. Now, as an executive building an event from scratch, he is giving creators like Williams access to physical spaces previously off-limits to media, like the warm-up room, because of their rapport with star athletes. Today, the coexistence of content creators and traditional media can breed tensions within press zones at sporting events, where creators like Williams compete with magazine and newspaper journalists for athletes’ limited interview time. (At the same time, traditional sportswriting is under pressure: Old stalwarts like Sports Illustrated have reduced their publishing schedule, while The Athleticsucceeded in its pledgeto local newspapers to “bleed them dry of their best talent” before being acquired by The New York Times Company.) Williams recalled that in Budapest, traditional media described influencers like herself as “fans with phones,” a perspective she disputes. “I totally respect and understand the form of journalism that track and field is used to,” she said. “Journalism is journalism. But I do think there is a way to do it in a respectful manner.” Balancing relationships with creators and traditional news coverage is something all sports leaders have to think about now. The NBA divides traditional media and content creators into separate press conference rooms, which Carney described as “complimentary and additive versus a source of friction.” But how much embrace of social media creators is too much? Jay Moskowitz, vice president of marketing and communications for Major League Pickleball, said influencers can be a great strategy for spreading awareness of a league—especially for startup leagues—but they should not be in charge of determining a brand’s identity. Therefore, MLP restricts creators to sharing five total minutes of content per four-day pickleball event. “If you don’t have clear media rules and regulations, and [you] instead let third parties run wild with your content,” he told me, “it can be hard to put the genie back in the bottle.” One example of third parties running wild are flourishing sports parody accounts that purposefully share fake news. One of the most popular such accounts, which covers basketball, is the anonymously run @TheNBACentel, which has more than 600,000 followers on X. (A typical joke: “The Bucks are reportedly considering legal action against Kyle Kuzma for a ‘breach of basketball expectations,’ per sources.”) The account was briefly suspended earlier this year—and jokingly mourned on many official NBA teams’ X accounts—before returning. Given that even parody headlines could have serious ramifications for the league or its players, I asked Carney if the continued existence of accounts like Centel means the league has a sense of humor about wider NBA discourse. “I’m not sure we have an opinion,” he said. Other sport leaders have decidedly less tolerance for parodists or any other digital pot stirrers. As the PGA Tour has worked to hammer out terms of a potential partnership with LIV Golf, a Saudi Arabia–backed rival, broadcasters like NBC have largely sought to avoid any controversy. “There are a lot of points of view in golf right now that are polarizing, and I wasn’t really interested in getting involved in any of that,” said NBC’s Tom Knapp. “We focused on the Good Good guys because they don’t have an agenda other than promoting more golf.” The same preference for amiable content is evident at Grand Slam Track, which is having its second meet this weekend in Miami and whose backers now include hedge fund billionaire Bill Ackman, among others. At GST, Williams serves as host of the intimate YouTube talk showSpill the Tee, where she promotes the circuit’s participating athletes, like Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone, world record holder in the 400-meter hurdles, and Masai Russell, a surprise gold medalist at the Paris Olympics. By now, Williams no longer has to fund her own travel as a creator, thanks to a bevy of brands who pay her to come to events—like Puma, which hosted her at the Paris Olympics. She has since participated in other creator programs with ESPN and the NBA, and she told me she thinks the future of sports media will include both traditional reporting and influencer content. “There’s room for everybody to do what they want to do in the space,” she told me. When she first started doing Instagram interviews at track meets, Williams thought athletes would prefer talking to mainstream reporters over her. Now, when runners leave the traditional media zone and head to the creator zone, “they’re like, ‘OK, now it’s time for the real fun—let’s really get into it!’” she said.

If Google were not ...
full_content: Mozilla earned $570million in revenue last year, 85% of which came from Google as a result of a deal Mozilla has to share ad revenue from Google search queries coming via Mozilla’s Firefox browser, the chief financial officer of the internet nonprofit testified on Friday. If Google were not able to pay Mozilla for search distribution—as the government has proposed as part of a broader remedy to fix Google’s illegal search monopoly—Mozilla’s revenue would drop “precipitously” because no other search firm could match Google’s payments, Eric Muhlheim testified. Muhlheim said that Mozilla had talked with Microsoft within the past year about what a revenue share deal could look like. Without Google’s payments, Mozilla would have to cut costs across the business, including investments in its Firefox browser, which could lead to a downward spiral of users leaving Firefox that could result in Mozilla ultimately having to go out of business, Muhlheim said. In response to questioning from judge Amit Mehta, who is overseeing the case, Muhlheim said that having another search engine of equal quality to Google that could bid against Google could ultimately benefit Mozilla. But, he said, Mozilla couldn’t afford the intervening revenue loss as they waited for that hypothetical competitor to catch up. Muhlheim also said that he thought that it was “not out of the question” that AI companies could become that competitor without additional remedies intervention.
