full_content: Google and MetaPlatforms have signaled they’re not seeing much pullback by advertisers worried about the economy, but it’s likely to be a different story for TV networks and video-streaming services. TV ad sales executives and ad buyers say marketers are already indicating plans to cut back spending on entertainment and news programming by as much as 10% in the coming year. Sports programming is likely to withstand the downturn, reflecting the value advertisers put on running commercials during live sports broadcasts appealing to large audiences, buyers say. That augurs well for Disney’s ESPN, Comcast’s NBCUniversal and Amazon Prime Video. Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Global are in a much more challenging position, ad buyers said, as their sports programming slates are much smaller in comparison. (Cable TV channels and smaller streaming services could be in an even worse position.) Netflix, which has the smallest sports offering and advertising business relative to its peers, expects to avoid most of the issues affecting its rivals. It isn’t seeing “any signs of softness” from its conversations with ad buyers, according to co-CEO Greg Peters during the company’s first-quarter earnings call. Netflix still expects to double its ad revenue this year, but Peters acknowledged that it  benefits from having a relatively small footprint in advertising. “That smallness probably provides us some insulation to the market shifts right now,” he said. The contrasting attitudes will play out during the TV industry’s annual upfront negotiations, during which advertisers finalize billions of dollars in ad-spending commitments for the following 12 months. These marketing showcases typically take place in May—Amazon is kicking off this year’s week with an event at the Beacon Theatre in New York on May 12—but negotiations continue through the spring and summer. Right now, as Donald Trump’s tariff policies are creating deep economic uncertainty, advertisers are primarily concerned with avoiding firm, long-term spending commitments, multiple ad buyers said. They will prioritize deals for ad inventory that may sell out quickly or whose price could rise sharply due to ad demand, buyers said. Both of those conditions apply mostly to live sports programming. Sports Edge That means marketers will strike deals with ESPN, which carries the NFL, the NBA and the NHL, among others. Comcast’s NBCUniversal in 2026 will broadcast the Super Bowl and the Milan Winter Olympics as well as NFL games, and it recently struck a deal to add NBA games.  Amazon Prime Video has also added NBA games in addition to the NFL games it already broadcasts. Even before the tariff issue raised the possibility of a recession, the TV industry was in the middle of a long-term decline as cable TV subscribers cut the cord in favor of streaming, prompting advertisers to gradually move money away from television. Much of that money is going to streaming, but some of it will go to social media outlets—such as Meta Platforms and TikTok—and some to other digital outlets such as Google. For all these reasons, Brian Wieser, principal at media and technology consulting firm Madison and Wall, said he wouldn’t be surprised if the total dollar value of spending commitments for this year’s upfront TV and streaming market falls by a double-digit percentage. “It’s already the case that TV is going through secular decline,” Wieser said. “When it becomes less and less critical for advertisers to buy, there’s no rush in making decisions and no rush in committing—even if there is still value in doing an upfront deal.” Outside of must-have ad spots during live sports, advertisers will demand flexibility for getting out of deals, ad buyers said. Historically, at the TV upfronts, advertisers have negotiated the option to cancel a portion of their future quarterly spending commitments—with proper notice. The way it would typically work was that for 12-month deals starting in the fourth quarter of the calendar year, commitments for that quarter would be 100% locked in. Advertisers could cancel up to 25% of their spending commitments for the first and second quarters of the following year and up to 50% for the third quarter. The notice time used to be at least 45 days prior to the start of the quarter, but in recent years that window has shrunk to 30 days. This year, some advertisers are likely to seek flexible options that hew more closely to the guidelines set by the Interactive Advertising Bureau, which allows an advertiser to cancel 100% of a commitment 14 days ahead of time, said one ad buyer. Amazon’s Impact Amazon’s decision to introduce ads within Prime Video significantly reshaped the upfront market last year,as The Information reported. This year, Amazon has sought to keep its momentum in streaming advertising going. It plans topush its ad-buying platform, which allows marketers to buy ads on its own sites and services as well as on other websites and apps. Amazon also has a shiny new object to show off: the NBA, which signed an 11-year deal with Amazon last year to exclusively stream regular-season and playoff games. That has opened up even more ad inventory during live sports programming, which advertisers are prioritizing more this year. Amazon has been looking to sell that inventory. In some cases, the company has been seeking to discuss ad deals that run over several years and provide marketers the chance to buy spots in many different sports broadcasts. Amazon’s sports offering includes the NFL’s “Thursday Night Football” and NASCAR races, among other sports and leagues. (Similarly, NBCUniversal has been shopping ad packages that include next year’s Super Bowl, the Milan Winter Olympics and its Telemundo network’s telecasts of the men’s soccer World Cup next summer.) Sahil Patel is a reporter for The Information, covering the business of media and entertainment. Before that, he was at The Wall Street Journal covering how advertising and media were being disrupted by technology. He is based in New York and can be found on Twitter @sizpatel.

full_content: Temu has discontinuedits direct-from-China shipping model and now requires China-based merchants to fulfill orders on their own when selling to the U.S. market.  The shift marks the online bargain seller’s latest attempt to keep its site stocked  as sky-rocketing tariffs make it uneconomical for Temu to send orders to the U.S directly. Temu has already been aggressively recruiting U.S.-based sellers since March last year, as threats of a favorable duty-free import provision disappearing were building, but hasn’t signed up enough U.S.-based sellers who can fill the void left by China-based ones. Temu introduced the new model, dubbed Y2, because the platform “needs a lot of listings,” according to a Temu livestream to merchants viewed by The Information. In order to attract merchants to sign up to the Y2 model, Temu allows sellers to set up new storefronts that inherit sales records and reviews from the direct-from-China stores, according to the livestream. While Temu still dictates the pricing of listings, it told merchants they can submit listing prices at four to five times of the direct-from-China model. Last month, Temu said it will hike prices for goods sold on its platform.

title: Nvidia Is Again Working on China-Tailored Chips After U.S. Export Ban
feed_content:
The U.S. government is steadily tightening the noose on Nvidia’s sales to China. But the AI chip giant isn’t giving up on the market.

Nvidia has told some of its biggest Chinese customers, including ByteDance, Alibaba Group and Tencent Holdings, that it is tweaking the design of its artificial intelligence chips so they can be sold to Chinese businesses without running afoul of U.S. export regulations, according to three people involved in the conversations.
full_content: The U.S. governmentis steadily tightening the noose on Nvidia’s sales to China. But the AI chip giant isn’t giving up on the market. Nvidia has told some of its biggest Chinese customers, including ByteDance, Alibaba Group and Tencent Holdings, that it is tweaking the design of its artificial intelligence chips so they can be sold to Chinese businesses without running afoul of U.S. export regulations, according to three people involved in the conversations. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang alerted customers about his plans while on a recenthigh-profile tripto Beijing. His trip occurred days after the U.S. government notified Nvidia that it was expanding the list of AI chips requiring approval for sale to China to include the H20, the most powerful AI chip Nvidia was allowed to export to China at the time. The move essentially banned sales of the H20 to Chinese companies. As a result, Nvidia said it expected to book a $5.5 billion write-down in the quarter ending April, triggering a sell-off in its stock price. Nvidia has repeatedly modified AI chips for the Chinese market over the past three years, since the U.S. started restricting sale of cutting-edge chips to China on the grounds that accessing the crucial technology will aid Beijing’s military rise. Nvidia’s persistence in coming up with new chips to sell to China despite escalating tensions between Washington and Beijing underscores how important China remains for the Santa Clara, Calif.–based chip giant. In 2022, before the Biden administration began restricting Nvidia’s sale of chips to China, China accounted for 21% of the company’s revenue. Since then, that portion has dropped to 13%. Even so, revenue from China grew 70% in the past two years to $17 billion, as Chinese companies showed insatiable demand for AI computing, just like their counterparts in the U.S. The H20 is the second China-tailored version of Nvidia’s Hopper generation of graphics processing units. The company reconfigured these GPUs to comply with U.S. export restrictions after the U.S. government banned the sale of previous versions to China. Chinese tech companies including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent ordered over $16 billion worth of the H20 chips in the first three months this year,The Information reported. It remains unclear how the recent ban will affect these orders. Nvidia told some of its Chinese customers it will need approval from the U.S. Commerce Department before it releases any new version to China, the three people said. Nvidia declined to comment. The White House, Commerce Department, ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent didn’t respond to requests for comment. Nvidia has told customers that a sample of the new chip, which will comply with the new U.S. rules, will be available as soon as June, the people added. The company also told customers it is still working on aChina-specific versionof Blackwell, its latest-generation AI chips, the people said. Nvidia must act fast to maintain its Chinese business before it loses sales to local competitor Huawei Technologies, which has developed chips and accompanying rack systems that someanalystssuggest are as good as Nvidia’s offerings—maybe better in some respects. Every time Nvidia has reconfigured its chip designs for Chinese customers, it has lowered the chips’ performance to comply with the latest U.S. regulations. But doing so inevitably reduces their appeal, especially in contrast with the rapidly evolving homegrown alternatives developed by Huawei. That is likely to occur with the latest redesign. Nvidia could downgrade the high-bandwidth memory inside the AI chips to slow down the data transfer speed between memories and processors. Another possibility would be to reduce the number of wires for the NVLink component, which facilitates data transfer between processors and other components in the AI chip units. During his trip to Beijing, Huang also discussed with customers how Nvidia can improve its Cuda software—which works with its chips—to better serve them, according to a person with direct knowledge of some of his meetings. Developers use Cuda to write code for managing Nvidia chips. While customers can run Nvidia chips without Cuda, they get the most out of Nvidia’s chips by combining them with the software. Nvidia has an edge in software over its Chinese rivals, as local competitors like Huawei don’t yet offer comparable products. In the meantime, Nvidia told two chip distributors that the Commerce Department has also banned the sale of its RTX 5090D gaming chip to Chinese customers, according to the distributors. Some Chinese companies haveused the chip for AI workloads, even though it’s not designed for that purpose. Nvidia told the distributors it was considering adjustments to the gaming chip, including possibly reducing its memory frequency, to make it compliant for sale to China, the two distributors said. Released earlier this year, the RTX 5090D is the China-customized version of Nvidia’s latest gaming chip, the RTX 5090, which the U.S. government has banned from sale to China since January. Qianer Liu is a reporter for The Information covering semiconductors and AI in Asia. She is based in Hong Kong and can be reached at[email protected]or @QianerLiu on X.

title: Judge Throws Out Some of Musk’s Claims Against OpenAI

full_content: U.S. District CourtJudge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who is overseeing Elon Musk’s breach of charitable trust lawsuit against OpenAI, dismissed 11 of the 16 claims under considerationfor a trial next March. The rejected claims included Musk’s argument that he had an explicit contract with OpenAI when he made early donations to the nonprofit overseeing the ChatGPT maker and that OpenAI and Microsoft had aided and abetted fraud. Justice Rogers denied OpenAI’s motion to dismiss other claims of Musk’s, including that OpenAI violated an “implied-in-fact” contract with Musk by attempting to convert from a charity to a for-profit company. Justice Rogers also rejected a brief thatformer OpenAI employees filedopposing OpenAI’s planned conversion, writing that it did not help clarify the legal issues in the case. Musk’s lawyers are due to file a response to OpenAI’s counterclaims by May 7.

title: Instacart Revenue Rises on Ad Sales, Order Volume
feed_content:
Instacart said Thursday that revenue rose 9% to $897 million in the first quarter, boosted by higher orders and an acceleration in ad sales.

full_content: Instacart said Thursdaythat revenue rose 9% to $897 million in the first quarter, boosted by higher orders and an acceleration in ad sales. The delivery company said gross transaction value for the first three months of the year rose 10% to $9.1 billion, slightly higher than the median of its own forecast, as customers placed more orders but spent less per order. The number of orders rose 14%, the fastest growth in 10 quarters. The average order fell 4% year-over-year to $110, which the company said resulted from subscriptions to Instacart-plus, which waives delivery fees on orders of at least $10, as well as restaurant orders. Revenue from advertising gained 14% to $247 million. Cash flow from operating activities rose to $298 million, nearly triple a year ago. Shares rose nearly 5% after hours.
